sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 covers the business centre of Westwood, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 28 degrees on the page so that Broadway and Center Avenue run up the sheet. It is bounded by Irvington Street at the top (only its south side drawn, the rest belonging to Sheet 3), Bergen near the bottom edge, Fairview Avenue along the east side and the railroad right-of-way and the angle of Washington Avenue on the west. Westwood Avenue crosses the middle of the sheet from lower left to upper right, lined on both sides by the downtown commercial blocks: brick and frame stores, the Westwood Theatre (moving pictures), the Pascack Theatre, the Post Office, a telephone exchange and department store, a Christian Science Hall, the First National Bank, the J. B. Speth Building, the A. B. Bogert Building, a bus garage, a printing works, a furniture company and a number of garages and repair shops. West of Broadway lie the railroad tracks with the passenger station, police booth and freight house, the Park Hotel and the Monarch Rug Cleaning Company at the angle of Washington Avenue, and a large blank area labelled Park, where the sheet shows only the north arrow and the scale bar. North and south of the business blocks, between Broadway, Center Avenue and Fairview Avenue, the sheet shows residential lots with frame dwellings and private garages, the Westwood Feed Company at the top, and a library and club house near the east edge. Water pipes of 6 and 12 inches are marked along most streets, and the sheet carries the September 1928 stamp of Westwood, N.J.
notes: Printed street names without a suffix (Irvington, Bergen) are Irvington Street and Bergen Street today.
Printed scale bar (0 to 150 ft) confirms 50 feet to an inch; the fit gives 7.9 px/ft.

The junction of Broadway, Washington Avenue and Westwood Avenue has no control point: the water pipes show Washington Avenue meeting Westwood Avenue east of Broadway, so the single OpenStreetMap node does not match the drawn junction.
50 ft. Broadway, Center, Westwood Av, Washington Av, Madison Av, Park Av, Irvington (top), Bergen (bottom), Fairview; railroad on the west. One part, turned about 28 deg.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 covers a compact block of central Westwood just north of the business district, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 28 degrees on the page so that Broadway runs up the sheet. It is bounded by Lake Street at the top, Irvington Street at the bottom, Fairview Avenue along the east edge (only its west side drawn; the east side belongs to Sheet 10) and Madison Avenue along the west edge. Broadway and Center Avenue run the length of the sheet, crossed midway by Grand Street, dividing the area into four long blocks. West of Broadway lies the right-of-way of the Erie Railroad (New Jersey and New York Division), with its main tracks, a siding and a track carried on a concrete trestle to dump coal; between the railroad and Madison Avenue is the yard of the Comfort Coal and Lumber Company, with a large lumber shed, a lumber shed along Madison Avenue, cement storage, piles of material, an office and a scale. Along the west side of Broadway, facing the railroad, stand several automobile repair garages, including a large auto repair building with a showroom and office at the corner of Lake Street, a carpenter shop, a blacksmith, a wood-working shop with an electric motor and a plumbing supply building. The blocks between Broadway, Center Avenue and Fairview Avenue are almost entirely residential, filled with frame dwellings and their private garages on long narrow lots, with house numbers along each frontage. Water pipes of 6 and 12 inches are marked in Broadway, Center Avenue, Fairview Avenue and Irvington Street. The areas beyond the edges are marked as Sheets 2, 7 and 10.
notes: Lake, Grand and Irvington are printed without a suffix; today Lake Street, Grand Street and Irvington Street.
Railroad lettered E.R.R. (N.J. & N.Y. Div.), the Erie Railroad; today the Pascack Valley Line.
Comfort Coal and Lumber Co. yard between the railroad and Madison Avenue.
50 ft. Broadway, Center Av, Fairview Av (east edge), Lake, Grand, Irvington, Madison Av; railroad and Comfort Coal & Lumber yard on the west. One part. Pilot sheet.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 covers the east side of central Westwood, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 28 degrees on the page. Fairview Avenue forms the west edge and joins Sheet 2 there; Irvington runs along the top, Bergen along the bottom, and Pascack Brook with the Hillsdale Township line cuts across the upper right. Kinderkamack Road runs down the middle of the sheet and crosses Westwood Avenue at the point where Harrington Avenue also begins. North of Westwood Avenue the blocks between Fairview Avenue and Kinderkamack Road, and the narrow strip east of the road, are residential, with frame dwellings and small private garages on deep lots. On the north side of Westwood Avenue, just east of Kinderkamack Road, stands a large garage built in three bays of concrete block with heat and electric light. South of the avenue a brick building with a row of stores faces the junction, and to the south and east the sheet shows scattered dwellings along Kinderkamack Road, Harrington Avenue, Park Place and Roosevelt Avenue, with Grace Episcopal Church on the corner of Harrington Avenue and a block of land marked Park enclosed by Park Place and Harrington Avenue. The upper right is open land crossed by the Pascack Brook, with the compass rose, the Westwood stamp dated September 1928 and the border of Hillsdale Township. The scale bar and the Princeton University Library stamp are at the lower right. Water pipes of 6 and 12 inches follow most of the streets.
notes: Printed street names without a suffix (Irvington, Bergen) are Irvington Street and Bergen Street today.
The Bergen / Roosevelt Avenue control point lies about 180 px beyond the bottom edge of the scan, placed from the drawn edge and street width.
Printed scale bar confirms 50 feet to an inch; the fit gives 8.0 px/ft.
50 ft. Fairview, Irvington, Kinderkamack, Westwood Av, Harrington, Park Pl, Roosevelt, Bergen; Pascack Brook and Hillsdale Township line upper right. One part.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 covers the area south-west of the business district of Westwood, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 28 degrees on the page. Bergen runs along the top, with Center Avenue and Fairview Avenue descending from it, and Broadway runs down the left of the middle with the right-of-way of the Erie Railroad (N.J. and N.Y. R.R.) beside it. Jefferson Avenue crosses the sheet diagonally from the upper left to the lower right, cutting the blocks into wedges; at its junction with Center Avenue stands the I. J. Demarest Inc. auto sales and service building. The blocks east of Center Avenue hold the Fire Department with its hose and truck companies, the I.O.F. Hall, The Fairview Apts. and many frame dwellings with private garages, mostly in the north-east. At the left edge the sheet shows First Avenue, Park Avenue, Elm and Prospect Avenue, with a Knights of Columbus hall and a block of dwellings, and the north arrow and compass rose in the upper left. Valley Avenue curves round a large unbuilt block of narrow lots in the lower middle, numbered 234 and 43 in the block numbering, and a street named Bank is lettered in the lower right. The lower part of the sheet is mostly undeveloped land laid out in lots, with a few houses along Valley Avenue. A scale bar is printed at the bottom left, and the Westwood stamp for September 1928 is at the top right. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches are marked along the streets.
notes: Printed names without a suffix (Bergen, Elm, Division, Bank) are Bergen Street and Elm Street today; the junction of Elm and Division was fitted as Elm Street / Carolyn Street, so Division appears to be the present Carolyn Street (not confirmed on the sheet).
Printed 1st Avenue is 1st Avenue in the OpenStreetMap data.
The 1st Avenue / Elm Street junction lies about 68 ft off the sheet and was not used.
Printed scale bar and fit (7.9 px/ft) agree with 50 feet to an inch.
50 ft. Bergen, Center, Fairview, Jefferson, Broadway, Valley, 1st Av, Park Av, Elm, Division, Prospect, Bank; railroad. One part. Division appears to be modern Carolyn Street (not confirmed).

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the north-western residential district of Westwood, drawn at 100 feet to an inch (the scale bar is printed at the bottom) and turned about 23 degrees on the page. The sheet is a grid of mostly square blocks laid out from Lafayette Avenue on the west to Brickell Avenue on the east and from McKinley Avenue at the top to Stratton Avenue at the bottom. Lincoln Avenue and Washington Avenue run across the sheet, with Wheeler Avenue, Clinton Avenue and Madison Avenue below them, and Steuben Avenue, Garden Place, Wellington Place, Trenton Avenue and Newark Avenue running down between them. The development is almost entirely frame dwellings with small private garages on narrow lots; the numbered blocks and lot numbers show it as a recently subdivided area, with a good deal of vacant lots, especially in the north and the south-west. A hall stands in the block north of Washington Avenue, a greenhouse and an auto washing building appear near Wheeler Avenue and Wellington Place, and a lumber shed and a carpenter shop lie beside 7th Avenue. In the lower right, 7th Avenue, 6th Avenue, Woodland Cross and Boulevard run diagonally through blocks of long narrow lots, with a few houses. The lower left and the bottom of the sheet are open land marked only by lot lines, with a second Lincoln Avenue running across the south. The compass rose is at the upper right and the Westwood stamp for September 1928 is at the top right corner.
notes: Printed Lincoln Avenue appears twice on the sheet (the upper one fitted to Lincoln Avenue; the lower one at about the bottom of the blocks was not checked).
Printed 7th Avenue, 6th Avenue, Woodland Cross and Boulevard in the lower right were not used for control; Boulevard exists today as Boulevard.
Lafayette Avenue / Wheeler Avenue was rejected by the detector (15.9 m): Lafayette Avenue is drawn slightly off the modern line near there.
Printed scale bar confirms 100 feet to an inch; the fit gives 3.96 px/ft.

100 ft. McKinley, Lincoln, Lafayette, Steuben, Washington, Garden, Wellington, Brickell, Wheeler, Trenton, Newark, Clinton, Madison, Westervelt, Stratton. One part, turned about -23 deg. Lower third (second Lincoln Av, Stratton) has no control.

sheet-7-1.description: The main part of Sheet 7 covers the west side of central Westwood south-west of the railroad, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 26 degrees anticlockwise on the page. It runs from the end of Grand Street and the Madison Avenue frontage at the top, across Washington Avenue, down to Mill Street and Stratton Street at the bottom, and from Brickell Avenue and 7th Avenue on the west to 2nd Avenue on the east. Washington Avenue crosses the upper third of the sheet; south of it St. Nicholas Avenue, Summit Avenue and Brickell Avenue run down to Woodland Cross and the Boulevard, and the numbered avenues, 2nd to 7th, run from Park Avenue and Elm down to Mill Street. A creek crosses the sheet from Woodland Cross to the south, and an open public park lies between Madison Avenue, 3rd Avenue and Park Avenue. The area is mainly residential, frame dwellings with private garages, but it holds several of the town's institutions: St. Anne's Roman Catholic School on Washington Avenue, St. Andrew's Episcopal Church, the Westwood Reformed Church on Park Avenue, the Calvary Baptist Church at Elm and 3rd Avenue, and the Westwood High School with its annex on 3rd Avenue near Mill Street. Industry is limited to a wagon shed and a blacksmith near Grand Street, a large public garage at Madison Avenue and 3rd Avenue, and the T. C. Bogert rushseat chair factory with its lumber shed and printing department on 4th Avenue near the Boulevard. The upper right corner of the page is taken by an inset, Sheet 7 part 2. Neighbouring areas are marked as Sheets 2, 3, 6, 8 and 9.
notes: Stratton St. is today Stratton Avenue.
St. Nicholas Av. is Saint Nicholas Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
T. C. Bogert Rushseat Chair Factory on 4th Avenue near the Boulevard.
Westwood High School and annex on 3rd Avenue north of Mill Street.
Residuals of 3 to 4.5 m along Mill Street and at 4th Avenue / Boulevard; not chased.
100 ft. Washington Av, Madison Av, St Nicholas, Summit, Brickell, Boulevard, Mill; inset top right (Park Av, 2nd Av, Elm) is part 2.

sheet-7-2.description: Part 2 of Sheet 7 is an inset in the upper right corner of the page, boxed by a heavy line and drawn at 100 feet to an inch with its own north arrow. It shows the single block bounded by Park Avenue on the north, 1st Avenue on the east, Elm Street on the south and 2nd Avenue on the west, just east of the area of the main sheet, together with the ends of Madison Avenue and the Erie Railroad tracks crossing the corner above Park Avenue. The block is residential: a row of frame dwellings with numbered lots facing Park Avenue, a few dwellings and private garages facing 1st Avenue, and on the corner of 2nd Avenue and Elm the Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church, a tile building with heating by steam and electric lighting. Six-inch water pipes run in Park Avenue, Elm and 1st Avenue, with a hydrant at each corner. The surrounding areas are marked as Sheets 2, 5, 7 and 9; the inset itself fills a gap between those sheets.
notes: Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church at 2nd Avenue and Elm.
1st Avenue / Park Avenue and 1st Avenue / Elm Street were hand-picked; the detector did not find them.
100 ft. Washington Av, Madison Av, St Nicholas, Summit, Brickell, Boulevard, Mill; inset top right (Park Av, 2nd Av, Elm) is part 2.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 covers the south-western part of Westwood, drawn at 100 feet to an inch (scale bar at the bottom) and turned about 29 degrees on the page. Stratton Avenue runs across the top of the main block, with Oakland Avenue, 8th Avenue and 7th Avenue running down the left and Mill running across the upper middle, where it bends north-east beside 7th Avenue. South of Mill the sheet is laid out in parallel east-west streets, Ash, Beech, Cypress, Euclid Avenue and West End Avenue, crossed by Clairmont Avenue and, at the left, Lafayette Avenue. The development is residential, mainly frame dwellings with small garages on narrow lots, thickest around Oakland Avenue, 8th Avenue and the Mill, Ash and Beech blocks and along Clairmont Avenue, Cypress and Euclid Avenue; many lots further south, in the middle and toward West End Avenue are vacant. A few long coop buildings stand in the open land north-east of the Mill and 8th Avenue block. The right side is largely open: a creek loops across the lower right and a long block of land numbered 120 and 148 lies between the streets and the east edge, where 4th Avenue is lettered. The compass rose is in the right middle, the Princeton University Library map division stamp and the scale bar are at the bottom, and the Westwood stamp for September 1928 is at the top right. Water pipes of 6 inches follow most of the streets.
notes: Printed names without a suffix (Stratton, Mill, Ash, Beech, Cypress) are Stratton Avenue, Mill Street, Ash Street, Beech Street and Cypress Street today.
West End Avenue is not in the OpenStreetMap extract and was not used for control.
Euclid Avenue / Lafayette Avenue was flagged narrow (Lafayette Avenue 40 of 60 ft) but its residual is 1.7 m; Cypress Street / Lafayette Avenue lies at the west edge of the scan.
Printed scale bar confirms 100 feet to an inch; the fit gives 4.0 px/ft.
100 ft. Stratton, Oakland, 8th, 7th, Mill, Ash, Beech, Cypress, Clairmont, Euclid, West End, Lafayette; creek lower right. One part, turned about -30 deg.

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 covers the area round Bogert's Pond in the south-west of Westwood, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 29 degrees on the page. The upper left is laid out in parallel streets, 4th Avenue, 3rd Avenue, 2nd Avenue and 1st Avenue, running up the sheet and crossed by Mill, which runs from the top towards the pond; an athletic field is lettered in the left of the area. Bogert's Pond lies across the middle of the sheet, with the outlet drawn as the Musquap Sink running east to Prospect Avenue at the right edge, and a smaller stream entering from the left. North of the water the blocks along Elm, 1st Avenue, Bogert Avenue and Division hold frame dwellings on narrow lots, with a block marked Park at the right. South of the pond a curved Goodwin Terrace and Gladys Place, Hurlbut and James run through a hillside subdivision of long narrow lots, mostly vacant, with scattered dwellings. The lower left is open land lettered Emerson Boro, showing that the sheet reaches the borough line of Emerson. The compass rose is at the top, the Westwood stamp for September 1928 is at the upper right, and the scale bar and a Princeton University Library stamp are at the bottom. Water pipes of 6 inches follow most streets.
notes: Printed names without a suffix (Mill, Elm, Hurlbut, James, Division) are Mill Street, Elm Street, Hurlbut Street and James Street today; Division joins Prospect Avenue where Carolyn Street does now and is probably the same street, but this was not confirmed.
The 4th Avenue / Mill Street junction lies about 66 ft off the top of the scan; OpenStreetMap has two nodes for it about 45 m apart.
Fit is looser than on other sheets (about 3 m RMSE) because the streets of the hillside subdivision are curved.
Printed scale bar confirms 100 feet to an inch; the fit gives 3.94 px/ft.

100 ft. 1st to 4th Avenues, Mill, Elm, Bogert Av, Division, Prospect, Goodwin Terrace, Gladys Pl, Hurlbut, James; Bogerts Pond, Musquap Sink, Emerson Boro lettered lower left. One part; curved streets, loosest fit of the atlas.

sheet-10-1.description: The main part of Sheet 10 covers the north-eastern edge of Westwood, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 28 degrees on the page. It reaches from Pascack Brook and the Hillsdale Township line at the top down to Irvington Street at the bottom, and from Broadway and the Erie Railroad (New Jersey and New York Division) on the west across Center Avenue, Fairview Avenue and Kinderkamack Road to Grove Street, Brookside Avenue and the brook on the east. Pascack Brook loops across the top of the sheet, crossed by concrete bridges where Fairview Avenue and Kinderkamack Road continue north into Hillsdale, and a second branch of the brook runs down the east side of the sheet below Lake Street; the borough line follows the brook and the area beyond it is lettered Hillsdale Township. Along Broadway, by the railroad, stand a plumbing and heating supplies building and a photographer's shop; otherwise the sheet is residential, with frame dwellings and private garages along Fairview Avenue, Kinderkamack Road and Maple Avenue, and large undeveloped lots between Broadway and Center Avenue and north of Maple Avenue. Lake Street, Grand Street and Irvington Street cross the lower half of the sheet between Fairview Avenue and Kinderkamack Road, with house numbers along each frontage and water pipes in most streets. The lower left of the page, behind a heavy line, is a separate part (Sheet 10 part 2). Neighbouring areas are marked as Sheets 3, 4 and 11.
notes: Lake, Grand, Irvington and Grove are printed without a suffix; today Lake Street, Grand Street, Irvington Street and Grove Street.
Railroad lettered E.R.R. (N.J. & N.Y. Division), the Erie Railroad; today the Pascack Valley Line.
Concrete bridges carry Fairview Avenue and Kinderkamack Road over Pascack Brook.
Fairview Avenue / Irvington Street was excluded: the heavy dividing line runs down the middle of Fairview Avenue there and the detector paired it with an edge.

100 ft. Main part: Broadway, Center, Fairview, Kinderkamack, Maple, Grove, Brookside, Lake, Grand, Irvington, Pascack Brook. Part 2 (lower left, behind heavy line): Washington Av, Koch Peak, Mountain, Hillside, Lafayette, Lincoln Av at the north-west corner of town.

sheet-10-2.description: Part 2 of Sheet 10 occupies the lower left of the page behind a heavy line and has its own north arrow: it shows a separate area at the north-west corner of Westwood, near the Washington Township line, drawn at 100 feet to an inch but turned about 66 degrees on the page, so that north points to the right. Washington Avenue runs up its left side, and from it Koch Peak Avenue, Mountain Avenue and Hillside Avenue run across the part, with Lincoln Avenue and Lafayette Avenue at the bottom. It is a lightly built suburban subdivision of long narrow lots, many still vacant, with a scattering of frame dwellings and private garages, a greenhouse and a few sheds; most houses stand along Koch Peak Avenue, Mountain Avenue and at the Washington Avenue end of Hillside Avenue. Six-inch water pipes are marked in Washington, Mountain and Hillside Avenues. Block numbers 58 to 61, 64 and 68 are printed in the blocks. The rest of the page, above and to the right of the heavy line, is Sheet 10 part 1, and the neighbouring areas are marked as Sheets 3 and 6.
notes: Drawn turned about 66 degrees on the page, north pointing to the right, against about 28 degrees for the main part of the sheet.
Koch Peak Avenue / Washington Avenue was not detected; five other junctions place the part.

100 ft. Main part: Broadway, Center, Fairview, Kinderkamack, Maple, Grove, Brookside, Lake, Grand, Irvington, Pascack Brook. Part 2 (lower left, behind heavy line): Washington Av, Koch Peak, Mountain, Hillside, Lafayette, Lincoln Av at the north-west corner of town.

sheet-11-1.description: The main part of Sheet 11 covers the east side of Westwood beyond Kinderkamack Road, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 28 degrees on the page. It runs from Pascack Brook and the Hillsdale Township line at the top down to Lotus Street at the bottom, and from Fairview Avenue and Kinderkamack Road on the west to Berkley Avenue, Bryant Place and the Musquapsink Brook on the east, where the land beyond the brook is lettered Rivervale Township. Westwood Avenue crosses the top of the part and continues north-east as Terrace Drive; below it Park Place, Bogert Place and Harrington Avenue run diagonally across a newer residential subdivision, while further south a regular grid is formed by Kinderkamack Road, Roosevelt Avenue and Lexington Avenue crossed by Bergen Avenue, Lowell Street, Jefferson Avenue and Lotus Street, with a short street lettered Bank at the lower left. Almost all buildings are frame dwellings with private garages. Institutions include a Methodist Episcopal church with a bell tower and a Masonic Temple on Bergen Avenue near Kinderkamack Road, and the Lyons Funeral Home on Kinderkamack Road between Lowell and Lotus. A concrete bridge carries Harrington Avenue over the Musquapsink Brook, and a stretch of Sand Road is drawn in the open land at the lower right. Water pipes of 6 and 12 inches are marked in the main streets. The upper left of the page, behind a heavy line, is a separate part (Sheet 11 part 2). Neighbouring areas are marked as Sheets 4, 5 and 12.
notes: Bergen (Av.) is today Bergen Street.
Berkley Av. is today Berkeley Avenue.
Lowell and Lotus are printed without a suffix; today Lowell Street and Lotus Street.
Lowell is drawn with a jog at Roosevelt Avenue; OpenStreetMap has two Lowell Street / Roosevelt Avenue junctions and both were detected.
Lyons Funeral Home on Kinderkamack Road; Masonic Temple and M.E. Church on Bergen Avenue.

100 ft. Main part: Kinderkamack, Bergen, Roosevelt, Lexington, Berkeley, Harrington, Westwood Av, Bogert Pl, Lowell, Lotus. Part 2 (top left, behind heavy line): Sand Rd and Old Hook Rd near the Emerson line.

sheet-11-2.description: Part 2 of Sheet 11 occupies the upper left of the page behind a heavy line, with its own north arrow: it shows an outlying area near the southern edge of Westwood, by the Emerson line, drawn at 100 feet to an inch but turned about 44 degrees on the page. Old Hook Road runs diagonally down the part and Sand Road branches from it to the north-east, meeting it in a Y; Old Hook Road is drawn 40 feet wide and Sand Road 30 feet. The area is thinly built: a few frame dwellings and private garages along Sand Road, a chicken coop, a large laundry building with a boiler room in the open block east of the junction, and on Sand Road the Mount Zion Baptist Church, marked as a coloured congregation, with another building drawn from plans next to it. An 8-inch water pipe runs in Old Hook Road. Block numbers 142, 155 and 213 are printed in the blocks, and the area to the west is marked as Sheet 12. The rest of the page, to the right of and below the heavy line, is Sheet 11 part 1.
notes: Mt. Zion Baptist Church (Colored) on Sand Road.
Placed from the single junction of Old Hook Road and Sand Road, with rotation from its drawn lines and the atlas scale assumed: low confidence.

100 ft. Main part: Kinderkamack, Bergen, Roosevelt, Lexington, Berkeley, Harrington, Westwood Av, Bogert Pl, Lowell, Lotus. Part 2 (top left, behind heavy line): Sand Rd and Old Hook Rd near the Emerson line.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers the south-eastern part of Westwood along the Pascack Brook, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 29 degrees on the page. On the left, Prospect Avenue and Broadway run down beside the railroad right-of-way, with a transformer yard of the Public Service Corporation at Linden Avenue between Broadway and Brookside Avenue and numbered blocks of narrow lots laid out between Linden Avenue, Brookside Avenue and Valley Avenue. A watercourse winds from the top centre down the middle of the sheet and then east to leave at the right edge, crossing under Old Hook Road and through a hatchery property. The upper right is a residential area of frame dwellings and garages around Lotus, Roosevelt Avenue and Lexington Avenue, with Palm, Fern and Brook Place cutting across, and a long diagonal street named Bank crossing a block of lots near the top. Below the middle, Kinderkamack Road runs down the sheet, crossed by Old Hook Road, Kingsberry Avenue, Lester Avenue and Crest. Along Kingsberry Avenue and Lester Avenue lies a line of dwellings and a row of attached stores, with a filling station and an automobile repair shop near Kinderkamack Road, and a fish hatchery building near Crest. The lower left is open land crossed by a dash-dot line. The compass rose is in the upper middle and the scale bar, a Princeton University Library stamp and the Westwood stamp for September 1928 are at the margins.
notes: Printed names without a suffix (Lotus, Palm, Fern, Crest, Bank) are Lotus Street, Palm Street, Fern Street and Crest Street today; Bank is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
Lester Avenue is not in the OpenStreetMap extract and was not used for control.
The Crest Street / Kinderkamack Road junction was rejected (9.5 m): the drawn junction sits about 10 m from the modern node.
A watercourse is lettered in part (Musquap) beside the compass rose and was not recorded as a place name.
Printed scale bar confirms 100 feet to an inch; the fit gives 3.98 px/ft.
100 ft. Lotus, Roosevelt, Lexington, Palm, Fern, Brook Pl, Old Hook, Kinderkamack, Kingsberry, Lester, Crest, Broadway, Linden, Brookside, Valley, Prospect, Bank. One part.
